description: A team from Sri Lanka at the Colombo event, taking on Planet X and SPHEREx. We're into astronomy, data, design and storytelling.
summary:
Star Shift turns NASA's SPHEREx infrared sky into a flip-book anyone can use. Type a star name or RA/Dec and the SPHEREx images of that patch play like a little movie. You can blink the first season against the last, subtract seasons to see what moved, and compare 25 years of motion across 2MASS, WISE and SPHEREx.

It doesn't just show pictures, it checks them. Star Shift measures each star's motion from the images and compares it with Gaia (Barnard's Star: 10.32 ± 0.27″/yr vs Gaia's 10.39), and shows honestly when something can't be measured. Click any moving dot and it checks it against known stars, JPL asteroids and detector glitches before calling it new. It even names the stars in your own phone photo and opens that patch in SPHEREx.

NASA says SPHEREx collects too much data for any one person. Volunteers comparing sky images have already found thousands of comets and candidate brown dwarfs. Star Shift gives curious people, students and amateur astronomers a way to explore SPHEREx and check what they find.
details:
Star Shift turns NASA's SPHEREx infrared sky into a flip-book anyone can use, then checks every claim before it shows you.

What makes it stand out

- Watch stars move. Type any star or RA/Dec and SPHEREx images play like a movie. Blink seasons, subtract them to see what moved, or jump to 25 years of motion across 2MASS (1999), WISE (2010) and SPHEREx (2025).

- Real measurements, not just pictures. We measure each star's motion from the images, with error bars, and check it against Gaia. Barnard's Star: 10.32 ± 0.27″/yr, Gaia says 10.39. The "How we know" page shows every result, including the ones that don't agree.

- Spot a mover. Click a dot that moved and it checks it like a scientist would: bad pixel, known star, known asteroid from JPL, colour. It caught asteroid 1354 Botha exactly where JPL predicted, in 8 of 8 images, and can write up a report for Backyard Worlds.

- Your photo to the sky. Take a night-sky photo on your phone and Star Shift names the stars in it, then opens the same patch in SPHEREx infrared. The photo never leaves your device.

- Asteroid Spotter. JPL's asteroids and comets in any field, with a zoomable orbit comparison.

- Lab notebook. Every number has a + button to save it, with a hypothesis template you can export.

- Light curves, spectra and signal-to-noise. Build a star's brightness curve, see its spectrum from the 102 bands, and measure how clearly anything stands out.

- Can I see it tonight? Tells you where to look from your location, and whether you need your eyes, binoculars or a telescope.

- Made for everyone. Simple and Expert modes, a quick tour on every page, colour-vision modes, a "Measure it yourself" class activity, GIF and video export, and shareable links. It even keeps working when NASA's archive is down.

Who it's for

Curious people, students and amateur astronomers. NASA says there's too much SPHEREx data for any one person. Star Shift lets anyone look through it and check what they find.

Benefits and impact

Anyone can explore real NASA infrared data without code or special software, and learn how astronomers actually check a discovery. Students can measure a star's speed themselves, teachers get a ready-made activity, and amateur astronomers get a tool to spot moving objects and check them before reporting. Our goal is more people taking part in finding brown dwarfs, asteroids and moving stars in SPHEREx data.

Factors we considered

Honesty first: every result shows its uncertainty and says clearly when something can't be measured. Accessibility: Simple and Expert modes, tours, colour-vision modes, phone support and plain language. Reliability: key stars are saved so the app works even when NASA's archive is down. Privacy: no tracking, and your photos never leave your device. Rules: all SI use is labelled and no NASA logos are used.

Built and checked

Plain JavaScript, three.js and a small Cloudflare Worker linked to NASA's IRSA archive. 474 automated tests, with our maths checked against Astropy. Open source (MIT).

Honest limits

NASA's archive was slow during the event, so unsaved stars can take up to a minute. SPHEREx has about 3 seasons so far, so distances aren't reliable yet. Very bright stars saturate and close stars blend, and the site says so wherever it happens.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

The idea, features and decisions are ours. SI tools (Claude, Codex, Gemini, ChatGPT for the logo) wrote most of the code under our direction and helped check the science and wording. Everything SI-made is labelled on the site.
